issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 21-year-old female whose trauma type is witnessing another person's trauma, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It does not plausibly connect to the other selected cues (blood, crash discussions) or to the rest of the profile unless there were a very specific female-linked circumstance, which is not reflected elsewhere.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Carry Weapon: carry weapon
issues.explanation: 'Carry weapon' is difficult to justify from the rest of the formulation and symptom content. There is no corresponding threat item or appraisal of current interpersonal danger, and the trauma is witnessing rather than direct assault. This strategy therefore appears to address a threat context not represented elsewhere in the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is poorly matched to a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, especially when no memory or trigger item suggests the patient herself was physically injured. This negative appraisal implies direct bodily harm and is inconsistent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Leila is a twenty-one-year-old forester, a job that once felt like a calling. She grew up in a tight-knit Middle Eastern American community, where she was known as the quiet, steady one who could always be counted on. She worked alone for long stretches in the Pacific Northwest woods, marking trees for harvest and mapping trails, finding a deep satisfaction in the solitude. That changed eighteen months ago, when she witnessed a logging truck lose its brakes on a winding mountain road. She was standing perhaps forty yards away, taking a soil sample, when she heard the grinding screech of metal and looked up to see the massive vehicle careen off the curve and slam into a sedan coming the other way. The sedan crumpled instantly. Leila ran to the scene, but there was nothing to be done. The driver of the car was dead. The logging truck driver was alive but badly injured, his arm bent at an impossible angle. There was a great deal of blood, and the smell—a mixture of hot metal, diesel fuel, and something else, something sweet and metallic that she still catches on the back of her tongue on quiet nights—has never left her.

In the weeks that followed, Leila returned to work, but the woods no longer felt safe. Every curve in the road, every distant rumble of an engine, made her heart pound. She found herself scanning the tree line constantly, looking for anything out of place: a fallen branch, a patch of loose gravel, anything that could signal another accident. She began to avoid driving on that particular road, taking detours that added an hour to her commute. When coworkers mentioned a recent crash on the news or discussed a near-miss on a haul road, she would excuse herself abruptly, her stomach turning. She could not bear to see a car with even a minor dent in a parking lot without feeling a wave of nausea. She became certain that she had failed. She had been there, she had seen the truck start to slide, and she had frozen for a crucial second before running toward the wreck. In her mind, that hesitation meant she had failed to protect the people in the sedan. She had acted in a way that went against everything she believed about herself—she was supposed to be the one who stayed calm, who helped. Instead, she had stood there, useless.

The memory itself felt strange, almost as if it belonged to someone else. When she tried to recall the moment of impact, she would hit a wall in her mind, pushing the image away before it could fully form. The smell, however, would come unbidden: while eating dinner, while showering, while lying in bed at night. To avoid the nightmares that she knew would follow, Leila began staying up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through her phone or watching television until exhaustion forced her into a shallow, restless sleep. She used to be a happy person, or so she had thought. Now she felt a constant, low-grade misery that she could not shake. She stopped calling her mother, stopped meeting friends for coffee. She told herself she was just tired, but deep down she knew she was afraid that if anyone asked what was wrong, she would shatter.

What finally brought Leila to seek help was a moment at work two weeks ago. She was marking a boundary line when she saw a smear of rust on a rock that, for a split second, looked exactly like blood. She dropped her equipment and walked two miles back to her truck without stopping, her hands shaking so badly she could barely grip the steering wheel. She sat in the cab for twenty minutes before she could drive. That night, she called a clinic and made an appointment. She is terrified that she will never feel like herself again, that the woods will always feel hostile, that she will always be the person who froze. But she is also, beneath that fear, hoping that someone can help her find a way back to the quiet, steady person she used to be.
